ch01.note: The word is yanyi (演义), the old tradition of the historical romance: real history retold and freely embellished for a popular audience, of which the fourteenth-century novel Romance of the Three Kingdoms is the classic example. Chen's disclaimer is exact—this is a factual record, not a yanyi.

'A martyr's death' renders chengren (成仁), an allusion to Confucius: 'The determined scholar and the man of virtue… will even sacrifice their lives to preserve their virtue (ren) complete' (Analects 15.9). The paired set phrase chenggong chengren (成功成仁), 'win through or else die a martyr,' became a byword for a soldier's two honorable ends.

ch01.anchor: a scale and half a claw
ch01.note: A set phrase, yi lin ban zhao (一鳞半爪), 'one scale and half a claw': all one glimpses of a dragon coiled in cloud, and so, by figure, any stray fragment of a thing whose whole shape stays hidden. The 'whole beast' Chen sets against it is that unseen dragon.

ch01.anchor: the thread that stitches the pages together
ch01.note: The image is drawn from traditional bookbinding. A Chinese book of the old style was xianzhuang (线装), 'thread-bound': its leaves were folded, gathered, and sewn together with a thread run down the spine. Chen casts himself as nothing grander than that binding thread—unshowy, out of sight, doing no more than holding the pages in their order.
